source: du Boulay, O'Shea, Monk (1981) The black box inside the glass box: presenting computing concepts to novices
finding: Coined the term notional machine while teaching Logo to children and trainee teachers. Built on Mayer's work. Idea: show novices an idealised machine implied by the language so the real machine stays hidden.
numbers: No numbers. Definition as quoted by Fincher et al. 2020.
quote: the idealised model of the computer implied by the constructs of the programming language
limits: Original paper not opened; known only through the 2020 working-group report. The authors did not test whether NM teaching beat another method.
agent_relevance: S2 trace on a concrete input should run on a small explicit machine for the language (what each line does to state), not on the model's loose sense of the code.

source: Fincher, Jeuring, Miller, Donaldson, du Boulay et al. (2020) Notional Machines in Computing Education: The Education of Attention (ITiCSE working group report)
finding: Working group defines a notional machine as a pedagogic device to assist understanding of some aspect of programs or programming. Four defining traits: purpose, function, focus, representation. An NM draws attention to one aspect and ignores others.
numbers: 12 authors; report pp. 21-50. Report says there has never been a fully precise definition.
quote: A notional machine (NM) is a pedagogic device to assist the understanding of some aspect of programs or programming.
limits: Broader and vaguer than the 1981 definition; Sorva 2013 narrowed it to program execution.
agent_relevance: Each trace step should name which aspect it models (variable state, call stack, heap) so the agent knows what it leaves out.

source: Fincher et al. (2020) literature review part of the NM report
finding: Review of papers that use the term notional machine. Most use it as background; few test it. Only about half define it.
numbers: 226 papers extracted. 116 (just under 50%) gave a definition. 72% cited NMs as related work, theory or motivation; 27% directly identified or used an NM in an intervention. 74 papers (33%) had explicit research questions; top topics: misconceptions/concepts 22, tools/IDEs 12, visualization 12, tracing/debugging 8.
quote: None focused their evaluation on the idea of NMs themselves, to test the theory.
limits: Search terms included close variants, but the review was limited to programming education.
agent_relevance: The evidence base for NM as a theory is thin: it is a lens, rarely tested. Test our own trace operator against plain reasoning (G7).

source: Fincher et al. (2020) citation analysis of origins
finding: Sorva's 2013 review is cited more often than du Boulay's original work, so many papers inherit Sorva's narrower, execution-only view. Many papers confuse teacher-made NMs with learner mental models.
numbers: Only 29 papers cited both du Boulay 1986 'Some difficulties of learning to program' and Sorva 2013; 49 cited only one of the two.
limits: Citation counts, not effect sizes. Mixing NM (teacher device) with mental model (learner's internal model) is a recurring boundary problem.
agent_relevance: Keep two objects apart: the machine we give the agent (NM) and what the agent really does (its mental model), which we can only check by running.

source: Fincher et al. (2020) section on idealisation and effectiveness
finding: NMs are idealisations: leaving things out focuses attention, adding analogy makes things comprehensible. An Aristotelian idealisation stays a true simplified model; a Galilean one distorts. Evidence on the educational effectiveness of NMs is limited.
numbers: Report says literature on effectiveness is limited; most evaluations look at individual mental models or at the effect of an IDE or visualization, not at the NM idea.
limits: Analogy NMs (parking lot for arrays, motorcycle for typed variables) depend on the learner knowing the source and can mislead.
agent_relevance: Prefer a true simplified machine over an analogy for the agent's trace (less room for wrong transfer).

source: Fincher et al. (2020) origin account of NMs (du Boulay and O'Shea, Logo)
finding: First-hand account: du Boulay worked with trainee primary teachers and O'Shea with school children, teaching maths through Logo. They did not set out to compare NM pedagogy with another pedagogy. Logo was harder to learn than expected for some teachers and children.
numbers: No sample sizes given.
limits: The founding use was descriptive and design-led, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: No founding evidence that an explicit machine model improves outcomes; do not claim it from this source.

source: Duran, Sorva, Seppala (2021) Rules of Program Behavior, ACM TOCE 21(4):33
finding: Proposes rules of program behavior (RPBs): teacher-facing statements of what must be learned about how a kind of program behaves. Rulesets are judged by viability and coverage and arranged in progressions.
numbers: Proof of concept: five rulesets for Python expressions, variables and functions. Coverage = share of programs for which a ruleset is viable. No learner experiment.
limits: Theory paper; authors say the effectiveness of rulesets still needs empirical comparison.
agent_relevance: A checkable model of S2: write the rules the trace must follow, test them by running code, and extend the ruleset when a rule fails to cover a program.

source: Duran, Sorva, Seppala (2021) Rules of Program Behavior, motivation and links
finding: States that missing viable knowledge of program behaviour is an obstacle to learning. Links to neo-Piagetian stages (Lister): a new ruleset can break an earlier understanding and send the learner back a stage.
numbers: Cites 'some evidence' linking conceptual difficulties to lower programming self-efficacy and hard-to-fix bugs; no figures given.
quote: The lack of viable knowledge of program behavior is an obstacle to learning and a source of frustration and unproductive failure.
limits: Mechanistic-execution framing is for text- or block-based intro programs; ML and embedded systems only mentioned as future work.
agent_relevance: Rules that always hold, whatever the program's intent, suit a code-run trace; apply the same stance to the agent.

source: Ma, Ferguson, Roper, Wood (2007) Investigating the viability of mental models held by novice programmers (SIGCSE) - as reported in Ma et al. 2008
finding: At the end of a first-year Java course many students still held non-viable models of assignment and object reference. Students with viable models did better on the exam and programming tasks.
numbers: N=90 first-year students (about 20 tutorials, 40 hours of labs). One third still held non-viable models of value assignment; only 17% held viable models of object reference assignment. Viable-model students did significantly better on exam and tasks (test details not in the opened text).
limits: Reported second-hand in the 2008 paper. Viability = matches how the concept works and always matches in use. Correlational; one institution.
agent_relevance: Even a basic machine rule (copy a value vs copy a reference) is often wrong; the agent's trace should state copy and alias rules explicitly.

source: Ma, Ferguson, Roper, Wood (2008) Improving the viability of mental models held by novice programmers (cognitive conflict plus visualisation)
finding: Teaching experiment: visualisation alone (Viz) versus cognitive conflict plus visualisation (CC+Viz). Visualising the assignment process repaired most wrong models; execution-flow models were harder to change.
numbers: N=60 volunteers in week 5. 18 held inappropriate assignment models (10 CC+Viz, 8 Viz); all 18 changed their model; 14 (78%) reached the appropriate one. CC+Viz 9/10 (90%) vs Viz 5/8 (62.5%). Execution flow: 12 held an inappropriate model; 6/12 (50%) changed to the appropriate one, 6 did not change.
limits: Cells of 8 to 10. No significance test for the CC advantage in the opened text. Volunteers. Authors say the importance of cognitive conflict was not obvious.
agent_relevance: Showing the real state change fixes simple state rules better than flow rules; S2 should show state after each line and take extra care with control flow.

source: Ma et al. (2008) discussion of why visualisation failed on execution flow
finding: Half of those with a wrong flow model did not notice it was wrong after the intervention. The authors say this explains why visualisation materials are not always helpful.
numbers: 6 of 12 with the 'Ss' flow model kept it. Pre-test: 10 held model ME, 12 held M2Ss, only 4 held other wrong models, so wrong models cluster on a few types.
limits: Small sample; authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Wrong models cluster: a short list of known wrong rules could seed a checklist of what to test in a trace.

source: Lister et al. (2004) A multi-national study of reading and tracing skills in novice programmers (ITiCSE working group)
finding: Twelve multiple-choice code-reading questions given to novices in seven countries. Many students were weak at tracing and at choosing missing code, which suggests a fragile grasp of skills that come before problem solving.
numbers: 941 students gave some data; 556 answered all 12 questions. Bottom quartile scored 0-4 of 12, top quartile 10-12. Q2 answered correctly by 65%, Q8 by 51% (third lowest). One institution supplied over half the data. 75% finished in under an hour.
limits: Convenience sample; MCQs without meaningful names or real-world context; quartile boundaries driven by one large institution; Q12 correct 67% at the base institution vs 38% elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Tracing is a separate, trainable skill that comes before writing; a trace step is a sensible gate before generation.

source: Lister et al. (2004) doodling and think-aloud analysis
finding: Students who traced carefully by writing variable changes got answers right far more often than students who made no marks. Not marking led to a correct answer only about half the time.
numbers: 56 students' doodles on all 12 MCQs. No doodles: correct about 50%. One fifth made no doodles on Q2; 55% none on Q8. Think-aloud guessing in about 10% of answers (half educated, half pure).
limits: Observational, not randomised; harder items may provoke more tracing.
agent_relevance: Human analogue of an S2 trace: written state-tracking raises correct answers; the agent should write the state table instead of 'seeing' the result.

source: Lister et al. (2004) misconceptions versus fragile skills
finding: Few errors came from misconceptions about a construct. Only Q6 (meaning of 'return') showed a frequent misconception. The authors read most failures as weak tracing and abstraction skill, not a wrong machine model.
numbers: Frequent misconception in 1 of 12 MCQs. One low scorer (5 of 12) confused an array position with its contents.
limits: Competing explanation to the mental-model account: errors may be skill failures rather than wrong models.
agent_relevance: When the agent errs on a trace, do not assume a wrong rule; compare against an actual run before blaming the model.

source: Dehnadi and Bornat (2006) The camel has two humps - as described in Ma et al. 2008
finding: Questionnaire on assignment where each answer maps to a mental model. Claimed that students who used one consistent model did well in the end-of-course exam.
numbers: As summarised by Ma et al.: most of the Consistent group (same model for all or almost all questions) scored a pass mark of 50 or above on the course exam.
limits: Second-hand summary. The strong claim was later retracted by Bornat (next line).
agent_relevance: Consistency of use of a model, not its correctness, was claimed to predict success; retracted, so do not use for the agent.

source: Bornat (2014) retraction of 'The camel has two humps' - Retraction Watch report
finding: Bornat publicly retracted the claim that the test split students into those who can and cannot program. He wrote that it was not a programming aptitude test.
numbers: In his answers: the retracted document was never peer reviewed; one related paper was at a peer-reviewed conference, the rest in lightly reviewed workshops. An earlier part-retraction was in Bornat et al. 2008.
quote: Dehnadi didn't discover a programming aptitude test.
limits: Page carries Bornat's own words; the failed replication itself was seen only as a mailing-list report.
agent_relevance: Warning for our literature: the best-known 'mental model predicts success' result is retracted; decide from outputs, not stories (G10).

source: Caspersen, Bennedsen, Larsen (2007) Mental models and programming aptitude (ITiCSE) - replication attempt
finding: Reported a replication of the Dehnadi-Bornat test with no correlation to outcomes. A reader on the same list argued it was not a true replication because predictor and response variables differed and results were pooled.
numbers: From a search-result summary only; no numbers seen.
limits: Not opened; disputed as a replication.
agent_relevance: Treat the Dehnadi-Bornat result as unreplicated.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for intermediate computation with language models
finding: Training or prompting a model to write intermediate program state line by line (a scratchpad trace) beats predicting the output directly. Early clear LLM test of an explicit step-by-step machine for program execution.
numbers: Synthetic Python, 200 test problems. Tracing table: direct 8.8% few-shot, 31.8% fine-tuned; scratchpad 20.1% few-shot, 50.7% fine-tuned. Execution table: direct 11% few-shot, 20% fine-tuned; scratchpad 26.5% few-shot, 41.5% fine-tuned.
limits: Early models. Few-shot scratchpad needed a relaxed scoring rule (model named the final variable v0 not output; under naive scoring accuracy was roughly zero). Synthetic programs.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S2: write the state after each line. The gain is large but absolute accuracy was still modest.

source: Nye et al. (2021) scratchpad on MBPP-aug, CodeNet and single-line data
finding: Fine-tuned tracing on real-style programs gets about a quarter of tasks exactly right. Combining training sets was best.
numbers: MBPP-aug alone 23.4% and CodeNet 25.2% tasks executed correctly. CodeNet plus single-line: final output right for 26.6% of tasks, all three examples traced perfectly for 24.6%, and greedy decoding gave the exact trace for almost 42% of all traces.
limits: Low absolute accuracy; one model family; exact-trace criterion is strict.
agent_relevance: Even trained tracers fail on about three of four real programs, so run the code for ground truth wherever possible (G2, G10).

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: a benchmark for code reasoning, understanding and execution
finding: Benchmark of 800 short Python functions with two tasks: predict the output (execute in the head) and predict an input. Twenty models tested. Models strong on HumanEval did not gain as much on CRUXEval.
numbers: N=800 functions of 3 to 13 lines. Best direct: GPT-4 67% input, 63% output pass@1; best open models 47% input, 44% output. GPT-4 with CoT 74.8% input, 81.9% output. Code Llama 34B 50% input, 46% output (abstract).
limits: Synthetic functions; pass@1 at temperature 0.2; contamination possible.
agent_relevance: Output prediction is exactly S2. Even GPT-4 with CoT misses about 1 in 5 short functions, so a real interpreter run is still needed.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: CoT and fine-tuning analysis
finding: CoT helps output prediction more than input prediction and helps the strongest model most. CoT hurts many single items for weaker models. Fine-tuning on near-benchmark data plateaus.
numbers: CoT helped Code Llama 34B and GPT-4 on both tasks, GPT-3.5 on output only, Code Llama 13B on neither. Confusion matrix for GPT-3.5 output: 159 items right without CoT became wrong, 340 went the other way. Fine-tuning Code Llama 34B on about 140K similar samples still plateaued.
quote: CoT does not seem to improve Code Llama 13B and GPT-3.5 performance on input prediction.
limits: Preliminary fine-tuning study; matrix count is read from the figure text.
agent_relevance: A step-by-step trace is not free for small models: test it against plain answers at equal tokens (G7).

source: Liu, Chen, Jabbarvand (2026, v6) CodeMind: evaluating LLMs for implicit and explicit code execution reasoning (IEEE TSE)
finding: Framework with three tasks: independent execution reasoning (IER, predict output), specification reasoning (SR, use a test in the spec when writing code) and dynamic semantics reasoning (DSR, keep semantics under a rewrite). 13 LLMs, four benchmarks.
numbers: IER: frontier reasoning models beat GPT-4 by 14.76 points (Claude-Sonnet-4.6), 11.35 (o4-mini), 9.26 (DeepSeek-R1) and the best open model by 35.70, 32.29, 30.20. RIER rose from 41.93% (CodeLlama-Inst-13b) to 47.32% (34b) and from 45.54% (DeepSeekCoder-6.7b) to 60.23% (33b) to 90.43% (DeepSeek-R1). Execution-tuned SemCoder-S gained 10.91 over its base.
limits: Temperature 0; numbers differ from CRUXEval because of prompt and temperature. Worst on Avatar (complex constructs), nested code, non-primitive types, intra-class dependencies.
agent_relevance: Execution reasoning is strong in frontier reasoning models but still falls with nesting and object state.

source: Liu et al. (2026) CodeMind: specification reasoning, gain from one test
finding: Adding one ground-truth input-output pair to the task spec raised pass@1 a little on average, mostly where the written spec was ambiguous.
numbers: Average +5.36 points pass@1; ClassEval +9.78, HumanEval +0.94. Repeat with unused inputs: +5.56 average, ClassEval 9.68, HumanEval 1.44.
limits: Two benchmarks only (the others lack NL specs); the ClassEval gain is attributed by the authors to ambiguous specs.
agent_relevance: A concrete example to trace helps most where the statement is vague; use S2 mostly then.

source: Liu et al. (2026) CodeMind: link between code reasoning and bug repair (RQ6)
finding: Before reasoning models, bug-repair success had no meaningful association with any code-reasoning task. Even when told to reason about execution, only frontier models (Claude-Sonnet-4.6, o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) used it to localise and repair the bug.
numbers: 13 LLMs; no correlation figure in the opened text beyond 'no meaningful association'.
quote: performance of LLMs in bug repair is not correlated with any of the code reasoning tasks
limits: Authors' framing; the table and Venn diagram detail were not read.
agent_relevance: A model that can trace in a test may not trace when it fixes; the program must force the trace step rather than hope for it (G1, G2).

source: Liu et al. (2026) CodeMind: DSR and complexity
finding: Size and instruction tuning did not predict ability to keep semantics when rewriting code. Execution-trained models did better. Complexity measures correlated negatively with reasoning scores.
numbers: SemCoder-S (6.7B, tuned on execution data) beat DeepSeekCoder-Inst-33b by 3.74 and CodeLlama-Inst-34b by 9.33 points on DSR. Rewritten programs grew by 39.73 lines on average.
limits: Spearman values not read; reasons are the authors' speculation.
agent_relevance: Execution-aware data helps more than scale; for a prompt-only agent the substitute is a real trace tool.

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: teaching large language models to reason about code execution
finding: Self-training on rationales that read execution traces improves program repair. Traces appear inline in the prompt.
numbers: PaLM 2-L fix rate +26.1 points absolute on Mbpp-R (23.2 to 49.3 with traces) and +14.3 on HumanEval-Fix-Plus. Without traces at test time: 19.0 baseline, 40.8 trace-trained, 44.1 trained without trace. Beats open LLMs by at least 29.4 and 11.1 points; on par with GPT-3.5.
limits: One base model; rationale quality by proxy metric plus human ratings.
agent_relevance: Showing real traces beats asking the model to imagine them; matches G2 (revise from real output).

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: CoT over traces in untuned models
finding: Just prompting for CoT over a trace did not help and sometimes hurt. Rationales hallucinated.
numbers: CoT dropped HumanEval-Fix-Plus by 7.8 points on average vs vanilla (DeepSeek Coder 57.3 to 30.5; StarCoder 29.3 to 16.5). Removing traces cost a further 4.8 (Mbpp-R) and 4.3 (HumanEval-Fix-Plus). PaLM 2-L rationales explained the error correctly only about 30% of the time. Their inline trace fits a 2K window for 95% of items vs 60% for the Nye scratchpad format.
limits: True for the models tested; the gain required training.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on free-form reasoning over a trace; give state tables and check claims against output (G10).

source: Chain of Code: reasoning with a language model-augmented code emulator (Li et al., 2023)
finding: Model writes code; an interpreter runs what it can and the LM emulates the lines it cannot run, tracking a state. A notional machine built as a hybrid interpreter.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard: 84%, a 12-point gain over Chain of Thought (abstract). Per-task numbers not read.
limits: Only the abstract and framing were read. The LM emulator can still be wrong on semantic lines.
agent_relevance: A design for S2: run exact lines in code, let the model fill only semantic gaps, keep the state in code.

source: Al-Hossami and Bunescu (2025) McMining: automated discovery of misconceptions in student code
finding: LLMs can name programming misconceptions from student code. Multi-sample mining beat single-sample. Many false alarms on correct code.
numbers: 1,063 code samples exhibiting 67 misconceptions. Best MCMiner-M (Claude Sonnet-4.5 with reasoning) 82.0% vs best MCMiner-S 78.5% (o3-mini medium). Bags with misconceptions 93.3%, correct-only bags 59.3%. Syntax misconceptions over 95%; 41 novel true positives (12.1% of bags).
limits: Samples made by an LLM injection tool, not real students; LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Naming wrong rules from output is feasible but over-flags correct code; do not let the model judge itself (G5).

source: Oli, Banjade, Olney, Rus (2024) Can LLMs identify gaps and misconceptions in students' code explanations?
finding: LLMs flag gaps in student explanations of code, but invent problems when the explanation is already complete.
numbers: 2,888 explanations (1,134 Java, 1,754 Python); split 75/20/5. Fine-tuning gave up to 15% over simple prompting. On complete correct input the LLM fabricated problems 27% of the time; on mostly correct explanations with small typos, 34% of the qualitative sample.
limits: Errors inserted synthetically by the authors; one lab; qualitative sample.
agent_relevance: A critic told to find faults will find faults; require a run-based failing output before any revision (G2).
